state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you explain why you think Fido falling asleep is represented by the negative-sloping section on the graph? How does this interpretation align with the concept of distance on a distance-time graph?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I thought that when the line goes down, it means Fido is getting closer to home, like he’s not moving or something. But now I’m confused because I guess if he’s moving back towards home, it should show that he’s actually moving, not just resting. Can you help me understand what the negative slope really means?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any other situations where a negative slope on a distance-time graph might not mean the object is at rest? Let's explore different scenarios that could explain the downward slope in this context.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the rest/movement confusion and maintains mathematical accuracy, but in Turn 3 asks the student to explore scenarios when the student has already self-corrected their understanding that negative slope means movement toward home (not rest), making the scaffolding somewhat misaligned with the student's demonstrated progress.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking, never provides direct answers, and in Turn 1 implicitly challenges the student's flawed reasoning by asking them to reconcile their interpretation with the concept of distance on a distance-time graph.
